summaries.example: Imagine two mystery boxes. If you are told that one box definitely has a red ball, you learn something. If you are told that a box has something that could be red, blue, or green, you learn less exactly. This shows why information is often connected with reducing uncertainty. But everyday speech can be confusing: people may call a rumor “information,” even when it is false or unclear.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of information asks what information is and how it works. In daily life, we use the word for many things: messages, data, news, instructions, or knowledge. These uses can conflict. For example, people may say they received information and therefore know something, but they may also speak of false or unclear information. Because everyday language is flexible, philosophers look for more exact ideas. Some mathematical theories measure information using probability and uncertainty. A message that was unlikely can provide more information than one that was certain. Other theories measure the length of a computer program needed to produce a string of symbols. Still other approaches say that information must be well-formed, meaningful, and true. These theories do not all describe exactly the same thing. The entry presents information as a large family of related ideas connected to mathematics, computing, physics, logic, knowledge, and communication.
key_ideas: In ordinary speech, information can mean data, a message, knowledge, or something that helps us learn.
Everyday uses of “information” do not always agree: information may be true, false, vague, or conflicting.
Mathematicians and scientists have created different ways to measure information.
One important idea is that a rare message usually gives more information than an expected message.
Some theories study meaning and truth, while others study probability, coding, or computer programs.
summaries.why_it_matters: We use information when we read, talk, search, measure, and use computers. Understanding its different meanings helps us notice the difference between data, knowledge, surprise, and truth. It also explains why one kind of information measure may be useful for sending messages but not for describing what a message means.

important_terms.definition: Facts, symbols, messages, or data that can be stored, sent, received, or changed.
Not knowing which possibility is correct. Information can make uncertainty smaller.
A mark, word, or sign used to stand for an object, idea, or relationship.
A mathematical rule for measuring information by how many possible choices there are.

questions_to_think_about: Can something be called information if it is false?
Why does a surprising message often teach us more than an expected one?
Does a picture or symbol have meaning by itself, or only in a context?
Is information the same thing as knowledge?

summaries.example: Suppose a communication system sends one of four messages with equal probability. Learning which message arrived removes more uncertainty than learning the result of a system that almost always sends the same message. Shannon’s quantitative theory captures this difference using probability and logarithms. However, it does not by itself distinguish between two equally unlikely messages with very different meanings. A semantic theory tries to add questions about form, meaning, and truth.
summaries.summary: The philosophy of information investigates a network of related concepts rather than one universally accepted definition. Historically, the term was connected with forming or informing, later became a general noun for data and messages, and then gained technical meanings in twentieth-century mathematics and information theory. Two recurring intuitions are that information is extensive and that it reduces uncertainty. Shannon’s theory formalizes these intuitions with probability and logarithms: an unlikely message has greater information value, and independent information amounts add. This framework deliberately abstracts from semantic content, so two messages can receive the same measure even when they mean very different things. Algorithmic information theory offers another approach: the information in a string is related to the shortest program that generates it on a universal Turing machine. This captures some patterns that probability-based measures miss, but the exact value is generally uncomputable and depends, up to a constant, on the reference machine. Semantic theories instead emphasize properly formed, meaningful, and possibly truthful data. The entry also connects these ideas with entropy in physics, computation, logic, knowledge, history, and the open question of whether the different theories can be unified.
key_ideas: “Information” has several historical and present-day meanings, including a process of being informed, a state of an agent, and data that can be stored or transmitted.
Technical theories tend to emphasize two connected ideas: information is extensive, and information reduces uncertainty.
Shannon information is quantitative and probabilistic. It measures message uncertainty without representing the message’s subject matter or truth.
Kolmogorov complexity measures description length. It can treat a patterned string as less informative than a random-looking string of the same length, but the measure is not computable in general.
Semantic approaches connect information with well-formedness, meaning, and sometimes truthfulness, creating a different focus from purely quantitative theories.
The source presents unification as an important research goal, while noting continuing problems involving computation, physics, meaning, and the relation between different measures.
summaries.why_it_matters: Information is a basic idea in science, technology, communication, and everyday reasoning. Different measures answer different questions: how surprising is an outcome, how compressible is a string, or does a statement convey meaningful and truthful content? Knowing these distinctions prevents us from treating data, knowledge, meaning, and truth as interchangeable. It also clarifies why philosophical questions about information reach into mathematics, computing, physics, and the humanities.

important_terms.definition: A broad philosophical field that studies information historically and systematically across mathematics, computing, science, and society.
A measure of information associated with probability; an event with lower probability carries more information when it occurs.
Information defined through the length of the shortest program that produces a string on a universal Turing machine.
An approach that treats information as data that is properly formed, meaningful, and truthful.
A property in which combined independent amounts can be measured by adding their separate amounts; logarithms express this relation for multiplication.
A measure of how unsure we are about which outcome or message will occur.
A model of computation that manipulates symbols according to fixed rules; universal versions can imitate any other Turing machine.
The claim that Turing-machine computation captures the general idea of algorithmic computation; the entry describes arguments for and against it.

questions_to_think_about: Should a false statement count as information, or should truth be required?
Why might the same message have a quantitative information value independent of its meaning?
Is the shortest description always the best explanation of a dataset?
What is gained and lost when information is represented as a set, multiset, or ordered sequence?
Can computation create information, or does it only transform information already present?

summaries.example: A messaging app can send one of eight equally likely stickers. Before opening the message, there are eight possibilities. Learning which sticker arrived removes more uncertainty than receiving a message from an app that sends the same sticker almost every time. A probability-based theory can measure this difference. But it cannot tell whether the sticker is funny, kind, or truthful. That would require thinking about meaning and context.
summaries.summary: Information seems familiar, but its meaning changes with context. In ordinary conversation it can mean data, a message, knowledge, or something that informs us. These uses do not fit together perfectly: people may talk about false information or vague information, while also treating information as something that gives knowledge. The philosophy of information studies this tension and develops more precise concepts. Mathematical theories often connect information with uncertainty. If an outcome is less probable, learning that it occurred can provide more information. Shannon’s theory measures this pattern and treats independent amounts as additive, but it does not describe what messages mean. Algorithmic complexity takes a different route by asking how short a program can be if it produces a given string. This can recognize regular patterns, although the exact shortest program cannot generally be found by a computer. Semantic information focuses on well-formed data, meaning, and truthfulness. The source also relates information to sets, sequences, coding, entropy, Turing machines, and quantum information. These approaches overlap in some areas, but they are not simply identical. A major philosophical question is whether they can be connected in a single broader theory.
key_ideas: People use “information” loosely for data, news, messages, knowledge, and material that can be stored or transmitted.
Ordinary speech allows information to be false, vague, or contradictory, even though another everyday use connects information with knowing the truth.
Technical theories disagree because they focus on different features: probability, quantity, computation, meaning, or truth.
Shannon’s theory says that less probable messages carry more information and that independent amounts can be added.
Algorithmic complexity asks how short a program can be while still producing a particular string, but it cannot always be calculated.
The source treats the relationship among information, computation, physics, and meaning as an active philosophical research problem.
summaries.why_it_matters: Digital devices constantly store, transmit, and process symbols, while scientists use information to describe uncertainty, patterns, and physical systems. Philosophical distinctions help us ask what a measurement really tells us and whether data alone amounts to knowledge. They also show why a theory that is excellent for communication may not explain meaning or truth.

important_terms.definition: The philosophical study of what information is, how it can be measured, and how it relates to knowledge, logic, science, and technology.
A way to measure information using the probabilities of possible messages or events.
The lack of certainty about which possibility will happen; information can reduce it.
A theory that measures the information in a message from how unlikely it is, without focusing on its meaning.
A measure based on the size of the shortest computer program that can produce a string of symbols.
Information described as properly formed data that has meaning and is true in the relevant account.
A collection in which order does not matter and repeated items may or may not be counted, depending on the type of collection.
A rule-based model of computation that reads and changes symbols; a universal machine can imitate other such machines.

questions_to_think_about: If a rumor is false, is it still information in the same sense as a true report?
Why might a very surprising message contain more quantitative information than an ordinary one?
Can a computer measure meaning, or only patterns and symbols?
Does putting symbols in a different order change the information they carry?
Why might philosophers want one theory that connects different kinds of information?
